chapters.title: Check-in and wins: Routing v3 beta and the outage response
chapters.gist: Maya leads with wins: the Routing v3 beta is at 11% fewer miles and 94.6% on-time across six fleets (uneven, about 6% in the dense urban fleet), and the team's outage response was strong even though the status page was late.

chapters.title: Team capacity and Daniel's burnout risk
chapters.gist: Maya says the team is running at about 110% and Daniel is a burnout risk after working the post-outage weekend and doing Harbor & Pine demo prep; Asher takes on making sure Daniel takes Monday off.

chapters.title: Tom promising live ETA to Harbor & Pine
chapters.gist: Maya learned via Daniel's demo prep that Tom is telling Harbor & Pine live ETA sharing ships this quarter; it's unbuilt, about 5 engineer-weeks, and competes with driver onboarding. Asher agrees it must be a planning decision and will talk to Tom before Friday.

chapters.title: Feedback both ways
chapters.gist: Asher asks Maya to push back earlier and more visibly in planning, with numbers; Maya tells Asher he says yes to too many stakeholders, and his 'let's see if we can fit it' reads as a commitment, which he admits is likely how Tom heard live ETA.

chapters.title: Growth toward Director, hiring loop, and commitments
chapters.gist: Maya wants to grow toward Director and will own the frontend hiring loop; Sam Rivera is a strong candidate heading to Asher's final round. They close on commitments: Asher talks to Tom and gets Daniel to take Monday off, and Maya brings a capacity model to Q4 planning.

turns.t: Hey. Hey, can you hear me? My headphones were doing the thing again where they connect to my laptop and my phone at the same time.
Yeah, I got you. Hi.
Hi. How are you? How was your week, or, I guess it's Thursday, how's the week been so far.
It's been a week. Honestly, I'm okay. I'm tired but I'm okay. It's been better than last week, which is a really low bar.
Very low bar. Subterranean bar. Did you at least get the weekend? I feel like I didn't see you online, which I took as a good sign.

I did, mostly. I went up to Point Reyes on Sunday with my sister and just, didn't look at my phone for like six hours. Which was amazing and also slightly terrifying, given the week. I kept thinking I'd come back to forty pages. But nothing caught fire. Well, nothing new caught fire.
That's the dream. Okay, do you want to drive or do you want me to? I had a couple of things but they can wait, they're not urgent.
Let me start with good stuff, because there's actually a lot of it and I feel like it all got buried by the outage.
Please. I would love good stuff.

So, Routing v3 beta. Kenji and I went through the numbers yesterday, it's the six fleets, everything since September eighth. We're at eleven percent fewer miles driven across the beta, and on-time delivery went from ninety-one point two to ninety-four point six. And it's holding, it's not a one-week spike, it's been basically flat at that level for two weeks. Kenji's ETA model is a big chunk of that, the mean error's down to four point three minutes from six point one.
That's, okay, eleven percent is a big number. Like, that's a slide. Is that consistent across the fleets or is one fleet carrying it?

It's not even, which I want to be honest about. The suburban and regional fleets are doing better than average, like thirteen, fourteen percent. The dense urban one is more like six. Which lines up with what we already knew, the ETA model still struggles with dense urban stops and loading dock wait times. Kenji's got a couple of ideas for the dock stuff, he wants to pull in historical dwell times per location. But even six is good. Six percent fewer miles for a grocery fleet is real money.
Yeah, no, even six is good. Okay. Can you send me the per-fleet breakdown? I'd want that before Tom starts putting eleven percent in every deck he sends out.
Ha. Yes. I'll send it today. And honestly that's sort of related to a thing I want to talk about later.
Noted. Ominous. Before that, how do you feel about the GA date? November seventeenth. Gut check, not the official answer.

Gut check, I'd say seventy, seventy-five percent. The solver's in good shape. The risk is the stuff around it, the migration path for the fleets that aren't in the beta, the settings UI for dispatchers, and the urban ETA thing if a big urban fleet is in the first wave. If nothing else lands on the team, I think we make it. If something else lands on the team, it gets a lot shakier. Which, again, is foreshadowing.
Okay. Lots of foreshadowing today. What else?

The outage. I know it was bad, forty-seven minutes, three hundred and twelve fleets, Brightside got hit really hard, their customers got wrong delivery windows. And the status page thing was bad, twenty-six minutes before we posted anything is not okay, and Ravi's already got that in the follow-ups. But the actual response from the team? It was really good. Ravi had the retry storm identified in, like, fifteen minutes. Daniel had the fix for the dispatch workers, the backoff and the circuit breaker, drafted that same night. The postmortem was blameless and it was actually useful, which, you know, not every postmortem is.

Yeah. I read it. It was a good doc. And I thought the comms after were good, even if the status page during was late. Sofia said Jordan at Brightside was, I wouldn't say happy, but he appreciated the writeup. He said it was the first time a vendor had actually explained what happened instead of just saying 'a third-party issue.'

Good. Yeah. So I want to make sure the team hears that from you too, not just from me. Maybe in the eng all-hands, or just a message in the channel. They know I think they did well. It means something different coming from you.

I'll do it. Honestly I should have already. I'll post something today, and I'll call out Ravi and Daniel by name. And Sofia, actually, she was on the phone with Brightside basically the whole afternoon, she took a lot of heat that wasn't hers to take. I want to make sure that gets seen too, because customer success always gets left out of the incident thank-yous.
Okay, so, that's a great segue, but I'm guessing the other side of it is, how's the team actually doing.

Stretched. Like, really stretched. We were already tight going into September with the v3 beta and the onboarding work, and then the outage basically ate a week for three people. And I don't think anyone's fully recovered yet. Ravi's buried in the follow-ups, the Redis config, the status page automation, the retry budgets. Kenji's trying to do urban ETA work and also answer every beta fleet question because he's the one who understands the model. Everyone's doing one and a half jobs.
Who are you worried about?
Daniel. Mostly Daniel.
Yeah. I figured you'd say that.

He worked the whole weekend after the outage. Saturday and Sunday. Nobody asked him to, I want to be clear, I actually told him on Friday to log off. But he was finishing the retry fix, and then he was helping with the Harbor & Pine demo prep on top of that, because Tom wanted the integration story to look really solid for Elena, the Samsara stuff and the Oracle TMS piece. And he's just, he's short in standups this week. He's normally the most patient person on the team and he snapped at Kenji on Tuesday about something really small, like a naming thing in a PR. Kenji was fine about it, but, you know, that's not Daniel.
Hm. Yeah. That's not him at all.

And the thing that scares me is he's our staff engineer, he's everywhere. If Daniel burns out it's not one person, it's like the whole architecture review process slows down, half the on-call escalations go to him, he's the person everyone asks. And he's not going to tell me he's burning out. He's going to tell me he's fine.
Has he taken any time off since the outage?
No. And he's got PTO, he's got like fifteen days banked. I've mentioned it twice. He says 'after v3.' Which is November seventeenth. That's seven weeks away.

Yeah, no. That's not okay. Okay, what if, let me, can I take that one? Like, I'll talk to him and make sure he takes Monday off. Not 'you should take some time,' like, Monday is off, it's on the calendar, it's done. Sometimes it lands differently coming from me, and it takes it off your plate.
Honestly, yes. That would help. He'll argue.
He can argue. I'll tell him the demo stuff is covered and that I'll personally deal with Tom if anything comes up.

Thank you. And I think part of it is he doesn't trust that things won't fall apart if he's gone. Which is partly on me. I need to get a second person up to speed on the dispatch workers so he's not the only one who can touch them. I was going to pair Ravi with him on the retry follow-ups, and that kind of does double duty.
That's smart. What do you need from me on the bigger picture, though? Like, is this a 'we need to cut scope' thing or a 'we need people' thing?

Both, but people don't help this quarter. Even if we close both frontend hires in October, they're not productive on the driver app until, realistically, January. So for Q4 it's a scope thing. I think we're running at, like, a hundred and ten percent, and that's fine for a sprint. It's not fine for a quarter. Which is basically the Q4 planning conversation tomorrow. And honestly, the thing I'd rather we didn't do is pretend we can do everything and then quietly slip three things in December.
Right. Which, okay, you said there was a thing you wanted to talk about. Is it the Tom thing?
It's the Tom thing. Do you already know?
I know there's a Tom thing. I don't know which Tom thing.

Okay. So, Daniel was in the demo prep for Harbor & Pine. And he came back and told me that Tom has been telling them, like Marcus, and I think Elena too, that live ETA sharing is coming this quarter. Like, 'it's on the roadmap for Q4,' in those words. Not maybe, not 'we're exploring it.' This quarter.
Ugh. Okay.

And Asher, it's not built. It's not started. We scoped it at about five engineer-weeks, and that's the optimistic version, that's without the edge cases on the tracking link, without load testing a public page that every end customer is going to hit. And it's directly competing with the driver onboarding work, which is a Q4 OKR. We have thirty-eight percent of new drivers dropping off before their first route. Priya's whole redesign, the phone login, the permissions primer, the practice route, depends on us having engineers for it. So if Tom's promising live ETA this quarter, either onboarding slips or v3 GA slips or Daniel works more weekends, and I'm not doing the third one.
No. Yeah. Agreed.

And I'm honestly, I'm frustrated. Like, this isn't the first time. It's a pattern. Sales commits engineering without asking engineering. And then I find out secondhand from someone on my team who happened to be in the room. If Daniel hadn't been in that demo prep, I would've found out when Marcus asked me about it on a call. Which would've been a great moment.

Yeah. You're right to be frustrated. I think, to be fair to Tom, the deal is real. Three hundred and ten k, it's the biggest deal in the pipeline, RouteWise is undercutting us on price, and the decision's October thirtieth. And Marcus has said live ETA is a must-have, more than once. So I get why Tom's reaching for it. And Marcus isn't the one signing. Dana Whitfield, their CFO, is the economic buyer, she's never been on a call, and Tom's worried that if Marcus can't go to her with a checklist that's all green, she just picks the cheaper option. Which, you know, is RouteWise.

I get it too. I'm not saying don't build it. Brightside's asked for it twice too, and with their renewal in January, honestly it might be the right call. I'm saying it should be a call. Made in planning, with the tradeoff on the table, not made in a sales demo.
If it came to it, though, if planning said we're doing it, what would you cut? Just so I have a sense going into tomorrow.

Honestly I'd want to look at the table before I answer, but my instinct is we don't cut onboarding, because that's a hard OKR and Priya's team has done the research already. I'd probably push some of the v3 GA polish to after GA, like the dispatcher settings UI could ship as a fast follow. And I'd want to ask whether Harbor & Pine actually needs the full thing on day one, or whether a tracking link with just the ETA, no live map, gets Marcus what he needs for Dana. I haven't scoped that, so don't quote me, but that's the conversation I'd want to have. With numbers.

That's really useful. Okay. So, I'll talk to Tom. Before Friday's planning, so tomorrow morning, first thing. I'll tell him we can't keep saying 'this quarter' until it's actually prioritized, and that he needs to bring it to planning as an ask, with the deal context, the dollar number, the timeline, and we'll make the tradeoff there, together. And if we do decide to do it, great, then he can say it. I'd also like you in that conversation with Tom, honestly, or at least I want him hearing the five weeks number from you in planning and not from me secondhand. Otherwise it's the same problem in reverse.
That's all I want. Thank you.
And if he's already put it in writing to them, in an email or a proposal or whatever, we need to know that too. I'll ask him directly.
Yeah, good point. Elena's going to hold him to anything that's in an email. She's very, she reads everything.
Okay. Can I give you some feedback? It's kind of related.
Yeah. Go.

So, I think part of how we end up here is, in planning, you tend to raise capacity concerns late, and kind of quietly. Like, I've seen you in the room, you'll say something like, 'that might be tight,' and then afterward, in a one-on-one, I hear 'that's actually impossible.' And by then it's committed and everyone's moved on. I'd love for you to push back earlier and more visibly. In the room. With numbers. Because when you say 'it's tight,' Tom hears 'it's doable.' When you say 'we have eleven engineers, here's what's committed, here's the five weeks this costs, here's what it pushes out,' nobody can argue with that.
Hm.

And I want to say, it's not that you're wrong. You're usually right. It's that the room doesn't get the benefit of it in time to do anything about it. Like, Q3 planning, the dispatcher bulk-edit thing. You said 'that's going to be tight' in the meeting, and then two weeks later it was the reason the beta slipped from August to September. If you'd put a number on it in the room, I think we'd have just not done it.

No, that's fair. That's, yeah. Bulk edit is a good example, I knew it was three weeks and I said 'tight.' I think I do soften it. Part of it is I don't want to be the person who always says no. Like, eng is always the no. Eng is the department of no. I don't love being that, and I think I overcorrect.

I get that. But numbers aren't no. Numbers are just, here's the cost. Then the room decides. If you show up with the table, you're not saying no, you're making the tradeoff visible, and then it's everyone's decision, not yours.
Yeah. Okay. Actually, that's helpful framing. I'm going to steal that. Okay, can I give you some back?
Please. Yes.

So, I think the other half of how we end up here is you say yes to too many stakeholders. And I don't mean, like, big yeses. I mean small ones. Tom asks for something in Slack, you say 'yeah, let's see if we can fit it.' Sofia asks for something for Brightside, 'yeah, we'll figure it out.' Leah wants a launch date for v3 for a campaign, 'yeah, that sounds right.' And each one's small, but they all land on my team, and they add up. And then I'm the one who has to go back and say actually, we can't. Which makes me the no person. Which is, you know, the thing I just said I don't want to be.
Oof. Yeah.
And I think 'let's see if we can fit it' sounds like a maybe to you, but to them it's a yes. Like, Tom probably thinks you agreed live ETA was coming. I don't know that, but I'd bet on it.

No. That's, you're probably right. I think he asked me about it a few weeks ago, in passing, and I said something like 'yeah, it's high on the list.' Which, to me, meant it's a candidate. To him, apparently, that's a roadmap commitment he can put in front of a customer. And then he's been carrying that around for three weeks, and from where he sits, product said yes, so why would he check with eng?
Right.

Okay. That's really fair, and honestly that one stings a bit because it's true. I think I do it because I hate being the bottleneck. Someone asks, I want to unblock them, and 'let's see' feels like the nice answer. But it's not nice if it turns into a surprise for your team three weeks later. So, I'm going to try to route stuff through planning instead of saying yes in Slack. And when I'm not sure, actually say 'I'm not sure, let me check with Maya,' instead of 'let's see.' And you can call me on it when I slip.
I will call you on it. Fair warning.
I know you will. Good. That's what I want. Honestly, if we both do our half, the Tom thing mostly doesn't happen.
Yeah. I think that's right. It's a two-sided leak. Sales hears a maybe as a yes, and engineering says tight when it means no. If we fix both ends, there's a lot less to clean up in the middle.

Okay, we've got, what, eight minutes. I wanted to make sure we actually talk about you this time. Last time you said you'd been thinking about what's next, and then we spent the whole hour on the outage.

Yeah. So, I've thought about it more. I want to grow toward Director. Not right now, I know we're sixty people, I know that's not a role that exists today. But I want to be working toward it, and I want the next year to build the stuff that gets me there. Like, owning more than just routing. Hiring, cross-team planning, that kind of thing. I've been an EM for almost three years now, and I think I'm good at running one team. What I haven't done is the stuff that's across teams, like, setting how we plan, how we hire, how platform and apps and ML fit together. And I think if I don't start practicing that now, then when the company is big enough to need a Director, someone from outside walks in and does it, and I'm kind of annoyed that I didn't go for it.

I think that's a great goal, and honestly I think you're closer than you think. The feedback I just gave you is actually part of it. Directors are the ones who make tradeoffs visible in the room. And, the capacity model thing, if that becomes the way we plan across all of engineering, not just your team, that's a Director-shaped thing. And I'd rather grow that from inside than hire it. So let's be deliberate. I can put together, like, a short list of what I'd expect a Director here to own in a year, and we can use it to pick the next couple of stretch things for you. Hiring's an obvious one.
Ha. Yeah, I heard that. I'd like that, actually.
What would be the concrete next step, from your side?

So, the concrete one, I want to own the frontend hiring loop. We're hiring the two senior frontend engineers, and right now it's kind of shared between me and Hannah and Priya, and nobody really owns it. I want to own it. Design the loop, calibrate the interviewers, own the bar, and make the hire or no-hire call with everyone's input. Right now different interviewers are asking totally different questions, and I think we're getting noisy signal. I want a written rubric, a real work-sample question instead of whiteboard trivia, the same design problem for every candidate so we can compare, and debriefs within twenty-four hours so we don't lose people. We're slow right now and good candidates have other offers.
Yes. Done. That's yours. I'll tell Hannah so it's clear she's partnering with you on it and you're the owner.

Thank you. And actually it's already going well. Sam Rivera, the candidate in Lisbon, Priya and I did the technical round on Monday, and they were really strong. Offline sync, really deep, like, the real stuff, not blog-post stuff. Great story about pushing back on a designer with data. The concerns are geospatial experience, which is thin, and about four hours of time zone overlap. But we recommended them for the final with you. And I think it was the first loop where Priya and I were scoring on the same rubric, more or less, and you could feel the difference. The debrief took five minutes because we'd seen the same things.

Yeah, Hannah put them on my calendar for next Tuesday. Anything specific you want me to dig into? And, to your point about speed, I'd like the decision within a day of that, so if we want them, we move fast. Can you and Hannah have an offer range ready going in, so we're not waiting on comp?

The maps stuff, and how they'd actually work with four hours of overlap. Like, how do they handle a fire at three p.m. our time when they've been offline for two hours. And yes on the offer range, I'll sort it with Hannah. I think if we wait a week we lose them, they mentioned they're talking to at least one other company.

Got it. Okay, let's wrap with commitments so we both leave with the same list. Me, I'll talk to Tom before planning tomorrow about live ETA. I'll make sure Daniel takes Monday off. I'll post something about the outage response to the team. And I'll tell Hannah you own the frontend loop.

And me, I'll bring a capacity model to Q4 planning. Eleven engineers, a table of weeks by project, v3 GA, onboarding, live ETA, the outage follow-ups, so everyone can see where the weeks go and what moves if we add live ETA. And I'll send you the per-fleet beta numbers today. I'll put the live ETA option in there both ways, the full five-week version and whatever the thinner version looks like if Daniel and I can scope it in time, so the room can actually choose.
Perfect. And in planning, put the table up early. Like, first ten minutes, before anyone's attached to anything.
First ten minutes. Got it.
Okay. Thanks, Maya. Seriously. This was a good one.
Yeah, it was. Thanks. Go talk to Tom.
Going. Well, tomorrow. Bye.

general.tldr: Routing v3 beta is at 11% fewer miles, but the team is at ~110% and Daniel is a burnout risk. Tom has been promising Harbor & Pine live ETA this quarter, so Asher talks to Tom before Friday's Q4 planning and Maya brings a capacity model.

items.text: Weekly 1:1: wins, team health, the live ETA commitment problem, two-way feedback, and Maya's growth path.
Routing v3 beta (6 fleets since Sep 8): 11% fewer miles and on-time up from 91.2% to 94.6%, holding for two weeks.
The team is running at ~110% after the outage; Daniel worked the post-outage weekend and is showing burnout signs.
Tom has been telling Harbor & Pine that live ETA ships in Q4. It is unbuilt, ~5 engineer-weeks, and competes with the driver onboarding OKR.
Agreed live ETA has to be a planning decision with the tradeoff visible, not a sales commitment.
Mutual feedback: Maya should push back earlier and with numbers; Asher should stop giving soft 'let's see' yeses that stakeholders hear as commitments.
Maya is working toward Director and now owns the frontend hiring loop.
ML ETA mean error is down from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes and drives much of the gain.
Gains are uneven: suburban/regional fleets at 13–14% fewer miles, the dense urban fleet ~6%. Kenji plans to use historical dock dwell times.
Maya puts Nov 17 GA at 70–75% confidence; risks are migrating non-beta fleets, the dispatcher settings UI, and urban ETA, and any new scope makes it shakier.
The Sep 24 outage hit 312 fleets for 47 minutes and the status page lagged 26 minutes, but Ravi found the retry storm in ~15 minutes and Daniel drafted the backoff/circuit-breaker fix that night.
Brightside's Jordan appreciated the postmortem writeup, per Sofia.
Asher will publicly recognize Ravi, Daniel and Sofia.
Ravi is buried in outage follow-ups, and Kenji is splitting urban ETA work with beta fleet support.
Daniel worked Sat–Sun after the outage on the retry fix and Harbor & Pine demo prep, snapped at Kenji, has ~15 PTO days banked, and is deferring rest until after GA.
Asher will make Monday a firm day off for Daniel; Maya will pair Ravi with Daniel on the dispatch workers to reduce single-person dependency.
New frontend hires won't help until ~January, so Q4 relief has to come from scope.

highlights.title: Routing v3 beta: 11% fewer miles, on-time 94.6%
Tom telling Harbor & Pine live ETA ships this quarter
Maya: 'you say yes to too many stakeholders'

ask.q: What are the Routing v3 beta results?
ask.a: Across the 6 beta fleets since Sep 8, Routing v3 cut miles driven by 11% and raised on-time delivery from 91.2% to 94.6%, with ETA error down from 6.1 to 4.3 minutes. Results are uneven: suburban and regional fleets are at 13–14%, while the dense urban fleet is around 6% because the ETA model still struggles with urban stops and dock waits.

ask.q: Why is Maya worried about Daniel?
ask.a: Daniel worked the whole weekend after the Sep 24 outage on the retry fix and Harbor & Pine demo prep, snapped at Kenji over something small, and keeps deferring his ~15 banked PTO days until after the Nov 17 GA. As staff engineer he is a single point of dependency. Asher will make sure he takes Monday off, and Maya will pair Ravi with him.

ask.q: What did Tom promise Harbor & Pine about live ETA?
ask.a: Daniel heard in demo prep that Tom told Marcus, and likely Elena, that live ETA sharing is 'on the roadmap for Q4'. It isn't built or started, is scoped at about 5 engineer-weeks, and competes with the driver onboarding OKR. Asher will talk to Tom before Friday's planning so it's decided there as an explicit tradeoff.

ask.q: What feedback did Asher and Maya give each other?
ask.a: Asher asked Maya to push back earlier and more visibly in planning, with numbers, citing Q3's bulk edit that slipped the beta. Maya told Asher he says yes to too many stakeholders and that his 'let's see if we can fit it' is heard as a commitment. Asher admitted he'd told Tom live ETA was 'high on the list' and will route requests through planning.

Maya wants to grow toward Director, building cross-team skills like planning and hiring beyond running the routing team. As a concrete step she now owns the frontend hiring loop, including the rubric, a work-sample question, and 24-hour debriefs. Asher will outline what a Director would own here so they can choose her stretch work.

ask.q: What did each person commit to before Q4 planning?
ask.a: Asher will talk to Tom about live ETA before Friday, make sure Daniel takes Monday off, post outage recognition, and tell Hannah that Maya owns the frontend loop. Maya will bring a capacity model (11 engineers, weeks by project, both live ETA options), present it in the first ten minutes of planning, and send the per-fleet beta numbers today.
